newsitem.title: USA: Rights group reports global increase in freedom.
newsitem.headline: Rights group reports global increase in freedom.

text.p: More countries were free societies in 1996 than ever before, the human rights group Freedom House said on Tuesday.

"The worldwide trend towards freedom and democracy is clear," the group's Adrian Karatnycky said in a statement. "Though many deeply rooted repressive regimes continue to resist this global momentum, the steady expansion of democratic values around the world is one of the most hopeful trends of our time."

Freedom House, a New York-based nonprofit organisation that aims to strengthen free societies, said 79 countries, 42 percent of the 191 countries in the world, are now free, the highest number recorded by the group since its annual survey began in 1972.

That means 1.25 billion people live in freedom, with 2.26 billion living in countries that are partly free, the group said. Another 2.26 billion people live in countries that are not free, according to the survey.
Regionally, Western Europe remained the most democratic area with 100 percent of its 24 countries free. The Americas were second, with only Cuba ranked as not free, it said.
Central and eastern Europe and the states of the former Soviet Union were seen as moving toward democracy, with the republics of Central Asia "dominated by authoritarian dictators," the study said.
Freedom House was encouraged by the increase in electoral democracies in Asia and the Pacific but disheartened by Africa, where only nine of 53 countries are considered free.
In the Middle East, only Israel was ranked as a free country, with Turkey, Jordan and Kuwait seen as partly free and 11 as not free.

Gains for freedom this year include the transition to a multiparty political system in Taiwan and a move toward freedom in the Philippines, where the influence of traditional ruling families and rebel insurgencies declined. Romania, Bolivia and Venezuela also joined the ranks of free nations.
Both Bosnia and Sierra Leone moved up to be classified as partly free nations. Setbacks for freedom occurred in Belarus, Niger, Slovakia and Ecuador.

The survey said the "worst of the worst" in terms of political rights and civil liberties were: Afghanistan, Bhutan, Burma, Burundi, China, Cuba, Equatorial Guinea, Iraq, Libya, North Korea, Saudi Arabia, Somalia, Sudan, Syria, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Vietnam.
